title: God prays (Berakhot 7a)
hookLine: God's own prayer: may My mercy overcome My anger
tomorrow: can a person bless God? one high priest did.

lines: MAY MY MERCY OVERCOME MY ANGER.
cards: Someone says something at dinner, and the heat is in your face before you've decided anything. Half a second, and the sharp reply is loaded. Berakhot 7a pictures God knowing that moment, and having a prayer for it.
In the Talmud's words, paraphrased: may it be My will that My mercy overcome My anger.

teach.b: The page asks: how do we know God prays? From Isaiah, where God promises to make people joyful in My house of prayer. Not their house of prayer.
Mine. So what does God pray?

teach.h: MAY MY MERCY CONQUER MY ANGER.
teach.b: In Rav's name: may it be My will that My mercy conquer My anger, that My mercy prevail over My other ways, that I deal with My children with mercy, and go beyond the strict letter of the law for them.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in the Talmud, God's prayer isn't for anything out there. It's about God's own temper. Now the debate, and it's an old one.
Read it as Maimonides did: God has no body and no moods. Anger and mercy here are images, the Torah speaking in human language, and the prayer is a model held up for us.
If God, so to speak, prays for mercy to win, so can we.

teach.h: KABBALISTS: REAL, AND WE'RE IN IT.
teach.b: Read it as the kabbalists did: mercy and strict judgment are real forces in how God meets the world, and the prayer shows them in tension, with mercy asked to lead.
On that reading, human prayer and kindness can strengthen the side of mercy. One reading says the picture is for us. The other says the picture is real, and we're part of it.
Both land in the same place: mercy over anger.

how: Jewish prayer often appeals to God's mercy; in the penitential prayers before and during the High Holy Days, congregations recite the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy from Exodus 34 together.

o: a prayer the priests said in the Temple for God
people praying to God on behalf of the whole world
the Talmud's picture of God praying for mercy to win

games.q: God's prayer and its two readings — tap the pairs.
p: may My mercy conquer My anger
an image; a model held up for us
real forces, and our kindness helps

s: in Jewish tradition, God only judges and never prays
Berakhot 7a says God prays, and gives the prayer: mercy over anger.
in Rav's name, God prays to go beyond the strict letter of the law
to deal with the children with mercy, beyond what the law requires.
Maimonides read the passage as a literal report of God's moods
he held God has no body or moods; the Torah speaks in human language.

games.q: you read God's prayer the way Maimonides did: an image for us to copy. now give the kabbalists' reading its best case.
o: mercy and judgment are real in how God meets the world, and our kindness can strengthen mercy.
God really has a body and moods, the same way people do.
the passage is a mistake in the text and is best skipped.
games.why: the kabbalists' strongest point: the prayer shows real tension, mercy and judgment, and invites people in. human prayer and deeds help mercy lead.

practice: Think of one person likely to annoy you before tomorrow. Picture the exact moment the heat rises, and plan one merciful move for it: a slower breath, a softer first word, a question instead of a verdict.
Rehearse it once in your mind, then hold it there for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: God prays. In Berakhot, God's own prayer: may My mercy overcome My anger, and may I go beyond the letter of the law.

orig.note: Hebrew: that My mercy may conquer My anger, from God's prayer in Berakhot 7a.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy over anger. Even God, the Talmud says, prays for that one. Berakhot, day seven.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 7a (how do we know God prays; Rav Zutra bar Tuvia in Rav's name: may My mercy conquer My anger)
Isaiah 56:7 (joyful in My house of prayer)
Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed I:26 and Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah 1:8–12 (God has no body; the Torah speaks in human language)
Kabbalistic readings of the divine attributes of mercy (chesed, rachamim) and judgment (din), e.g. the Zohar
